Chapter overview

Twentieth-century Tamil socio-political movements transformed reform into organised representation through associations, parties, unions, legislation, women’s organisations, temple-entry campaigns, language politics and mass Dravidian mobilisation.

Non-Brahmin organisationSocial representationLabour & agrarian politicsWomen & temple entryLanguage & Dravidian transition
Scope, Historical Context and Major Phases

Twentieth-century Tamil socio-political movements converted nineteenth-century reform foundations into parties, unions, elections, legislation, mass protest and organised claims for social representation.

Scope

Twentieth-century socio-political movements in Tamil Nadu emerged from the interaction of:

  • Colonial administration
  • Modern education
  • Caste inequality
  • Unequal access to government employment
  • Growth of newspapers
  • Expansion of representative institutions
  • Urbanisation
  • Industrial labour
  • Women’s political participation
  • Language consciousness
  • Anti-caste thought
  • Nationalism
  • Socialism
  • Rationalism

The movements were not organised around one single objective.

Some demanded:

  • Political independence

Others prioritised:

  • Social equality
  • Communal representation
  • Education
  • Public employment
  • Temple entry
  • Women’s rights
  • Labour rights
  • Language protection
  • Caste eradication
Transformation from the Nineteenth Century

Nineteenth-century reformers often worked through:

  • Religious movements
  • Missionary schools
  • Charitable institutions
  • Literary revival
  • Community preaching

Twentieth-century movements increasingly used:

  • Political parties
  • Registered associations
  • Trade unions
  • Elections
  • Legislative councils
  • Newspapers
  • Public conferences
  • Mass demonstrations
  • Picketing
  • Court cases
  • Government orders
Broad Phases
Early Organisational Phase

Approximately 1900–1916:

  • Community associations
  • Non-Brahmin organisations
  • Adi Dravida associations
  • Educational hostels
  • Print-based mobilisation
Representative-Politics Phase

From 1916:

  • South Indian Liberal Federation
  • Non-Brahmin Manifesto
  • Elections under dyarchy
  • Communal representation
  • Women’s franchise
Mass Social-Movement Phase

From the 1920s:

  • Labour mobilisation
  • Self-Respect ideas
  • Temple-entry campaigns
  • Women’s political participation
  • Anti-Hindi agitation
  • Peasant organisation
Dravidian Political Transition

From the 1940s:

  • Justice Party transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam
  • Dravidian social ideology expanded
  • DMK formed in 1949
  • Electoral Dravidian politics grew after Independence

Detailed treatment of these later transitions belongs to Chapters 22–29.

Sources

Important sources include:

  • Association records
  • Legislative proceedings
  • Government Orders
  • Election records
  • Newspapers
  • Party publications
  • Trade-union documents
  • Conference resolutions
  • Court records
  • Speeches
  • Autobiographies
  • Community histories
  • Oral testimony

Movement publications often reflect their own political positions. Colonial reports may describe protest as disorder. Both require careful comparison.

Early Non-Brahmin Associations and the Dravidian Association

Early non-Brahmin associations transformed inequalities in education, employment and urban accommodation into an organised Dravidian social and political platform.

Background

Western education and colonial administration created new government and professional opportunities.

However, many non-Brahmin leaders believed that access to:

  • Government employment
  • Higher education
  • Legal professions
  • Administrative posts
  • Representative institutions

was distributed unequally.

This produced organised demands for communal representation and educational access.

Madras Non-Brahmin Association

The Madras Non-Brahmin Association was founded in 1909.

Its founders included:

  • P. Subramaniam
  • M. Purushothama Naidu

The association attempted to:

  • Unite non-Brahmin communities
  • Improve access to education
  • Increase representation in government employment
  • Express grievances against administrative inequality

Its early influence remained limited, but it helped establish the idea of organised non-Brahmin politics.

Madras United League

The Madras United League was founded in 1912.

It was associated with non-Brahmin government employees who believed they faced discrimination in promotions and appointments.

Important leader:

  • Dr. C. Natesa Mudaliar

Its activities included:

  • Adult-education classes
  • Support for non-Brahmin graduates
  • Discussion of public-employment inequalities
  • Building links between different non-Brahmin communities
Madras Dravidian Association

The Madras United League was renamed the:

  • Madras Dravidian Association

The change occurred during the organisation’s early development, commonly associated with 1912–1913.

The term “Dravidian” was used to create a broader identity among non-Brahmin communities of South India.

Dravidian Home

C. Natesa Mudaliar established the:

  • Dravidian Home
  • At Triplicane in Madras

The hostel was created because many non-Brahmin students faced discrimination when seeking food and accommodation in the city.

The institution provided:

  • Hostel facilities
  • Educational support
  • Social networks
  • Political awareness
Importance

These organisations transformed private grievances into public demands.

They created the organisational foundation for:

  • South Indian Liberal Federation
  • Justice Party
  • Communal representation
  • Later Dravidian politics

The complete career of C. Natesa Mudaliar and the Justice Party belongs to Chapter 22.

South Indian Liberal Federation and the Non-Brahmin Manifesto

The South Indian Liberal Federation and its Non-Brahmin Manifesto converted non-Brahmin mobilisation into a provincial electoral organisation popularly called the Justice Party.

Formation

In November 1916, prominent non-Brahmin leaders met in Madras and established the:

  • South Indian Liberal Federation

It became popularly known as the:

  • Justice Party

Principal founders included:

  • P. Theagaraya Chetty
  • Dr. T. M. Nair
  • Dr. C. Natesa Mudaliar

The organisation sought to represent non-Brahmin interests in the Madras Presidency.

South Indian People’s Association

A related organisation called the:

  • South Indian People’s Association

was created as the movement’s publication and propaganda body.

Its purpose was to publish newspapers in:

  • English
  • Tamil
  • Telugu
Non-Brahmin Manifesto

The Non-Brahmin Manifesto was issued in December 1916.

It argued that:

  • Government employment was unequally distributed.
  • Legislative representation should reflect different communities.
  • Education should be more widely accessible.
  • Political reforms should not transfer power to one socially dominant group.
  • Non-Brahmin communities required independent organisation.

The manifesto treated communal representation as protection against administrative monopoly.

Justice Newspaper

The English newspaper:

  • Justice

began publication on:

  • 26 February 1917

Dr. T. M. Nair became closely associated with its editorial direction.

Other movement publications included Tamil and Telugu newspapers.

Electoral Politics

The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced dyarchy and expanded provincial elections.

The Justice Party:

  • Contested the 1920 election
  • Won a majority in the Madras Legislative Council
  • Formed the first ministry under the new system
Chapter Boundary

This topic covers only:

  • Origin
  • Manifesto
  • Organisational transition
  • Entry into elections

Detailed treatment of:

  • Ministries
  • Chief ministers
  • Laws
  • Educational reforms
  • Communal Government Orders
  • Decline of the party

belongs to Chapter 22.

Communal Representation, Education and Public Employment

Communal representation developed as a corrective response to unequal access to education and public employment and became a major precursor of Tamil Nadu’s reservation policy.

Meaning of Communal Representation

In the Madras Presidency, the word “communal” referred to the distribution of opportunities among recognised social and religious communities.

The policy aimed to prevent one community from securing a disproportionate share of:

  • Government employment
  • Educational admissions
  • Legislative representation
Basis of the Demand

Supporters argued that formal equality was insufficient because different communities had unequal historical access to:

  • English education
  • Colleges
  • Professional qualifications
  • Administrative networks
  • Government employment

They therefore demanded group-based representation.

First Communal Government Order

The Justice Party government issued an important Communal Government Order in 1921.

It sought to distribute public appointments among communities such as:

  • Non-Brahmin Hindus
  • Brahmins
  • Muslims
  • Indian Christians and Anglo-Indians
  • Depressed Classes

The order was revised and implemented more effectively through later measures.

Muthiah Mudaliar and the 1928 Order

In 1928, S. Muthiah Mudaliar, Education Minister in the P. Subbarayan government, introduced a more effective communal allocation system.

The system attempted to ensure that public appointments were distributed rather than monopolised.

Education

The social-justice debate also concerned:

  • College admissions
  • Scholarships
  • Hostels
  • School access
  • Representation in professional education

Educational institutions became central because public employment often required formal qualifications.

Historical Significance

The Communal G.O. became an important predecessor of later reservation policy in Tamil Nadu.

It introduced the principle that:

  • Unequal social groups might require differentiated state support
  • Representation should be measured across communities
  • Merit could not be separated from unequal access to education
Historical Debate

Supporters viewed communal representation as:

  • Social justice
  • Corrective representation
  • Protection for excluded communities

Critics viewed it as:

  • Caste-based politics
  • Administrative division
  • A challenge to individual competition

Detailed orders, ratios and Justice Party debates belong to Chapter 22.

Adi Dravida Political Mobilisation and M. C. Rajah

Adi Dravida mobilisation demanded safeguards independent of broader non-Brahmin politics, with M. C. Rajah emphasising education, employment and legislative representation.

Continuity from the Nineteenth Century

Twentieth-century Adi Dravida politics developed from earlier movements led by:

  • Iyothee Thass
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan
  • Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha
  • Dravida Mahajana Sabha
  • Buddhist associations
  • Community newspapers

Detailed nineteenth-century origins belong to Chapter 20.

Meaning of Adi Dravida

The term Adi Dravida was promoted as an alternative to insulting or externally imposed caste labels.

It conveyed the idea that oppressed communities were:

  • Original inhabitants
  • Ancient Dravidians
  • Entitled to dignity
  • A distinct political community

The term gained official and political currency during the twentieth century.

M. C. Rajah

Mylai Chinnathambi Pillai Rajah is commonly known as:

  • M. C. Rajah

He was born in 1883 and became an important leader of the Depressed Classes.

His work focused on:

  • Education
  • Government employment
  • Legislative representation
  • Removal of caste disabilities
  • Political safeguards
Organisational Role

M. C. Rajah became associated with the:

  • Adi Dravida Mahajana Sabha
  • Depressed Classes organisations

He helped submit demands to constitutional-reform bodies.

Legislative Representation

Rajah entered the Madras Legislative Council during the early representative phase.

He later became an important all-India spokesperson for the Depressed Classes.

His interventions demanded:

  • Reserved representation
  • Scholarships
  • School access
  • Government employment
  • Protection against untouchability
  • Representation in local bodies
Rajah–Moonje Pact

In 1932, M. C. Rajah entered into an agreement with:

  • B. S. Moonje

The Rajah–Moonje Pact accepted joint electorates with reserved seats for the Depressed Classes.

It preceded the Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar.

Rajah and Ambedkar

M. C. Rajah and B. R. Ambedkar shared the objective of securing political safeguards for oppressed communities.

However, they sometimes differed over:

  • Separate electorates
  • Joint electorates
  • Political alliances
  • Representation strategy
Rettamalai Srinivasan

Rettamalai Srinivasan continued his political activity during the twentieth century.

Important associations included:

  • Depressed Classes representation
  • Legislative activity
  • Round Table Conferences
  • Participation in constitutional negotiations
Importance

Adi Dravida politics developed independently from the broader non-Brahmin movement.

The two movements sometimes cooperated, but their interests were not identical.

Non-Brahmin representation did not automatically guarantee adequate representation for the most oppressed communities.

Community Associations and Social Mobility

Community associations used schools, hostels, commerce and mutual support to promote social mobility, while also retaining and sometimes strengthening caste-based organisation.

Rise of Community Organisations

During the twentieth century, many communities established formal organisations to promote:

  • Education
  • Employment
  • Scholarships
  • Hostels
  • Marriage reform
  • Commercial cooperation
  • Political representation
  • Social status

These associations were shaped by:

  • Census classification
  • Electoral politics
  • Modern education
  • Urban migration
  • Print communication
  • Competition for public employment
Nadar Mahajana Sangam

The Nadar Mahajana Sangam was founded in 1910.

It is associated with:

  • T. Ratnasamy Nadar
  • Other prominent members of the Nadar community

Its objectives included:

  • Community unity
  • Educational advancement
  • Scholarships
  • Commercial development
  • Social reform
  • Protection of community interests

The Sangam established or supported:

  • Schools
  • Colleges
  • Local associations
  • Hostels
  • Charitable institutions
Economic Organisation

Nadar commercial networks helped create institutions including the banking enterprise that later developed into:

  • Tamilnad Mercantile Bank

Community economic cooperation supported:

  • Trade
  • Education
  • Social mobility
  • Urbanisation
Other Community Associations

Different caste and occupational communities established organisations for:

  • Sanskritisation or status claims
  • Educational uplift
  • Political representation
  • Community publications
  • Marriage regulation
  • Economic mutual aid

These included associations among:

  • Vanniyars
  • Viswakarmas
  • Sengunthars
  • Yadavas
  • Naidus
  • Chettiars
  • Muslim communities
  • Christian communities
  • Adi Dravidars
Benefits

Community associations helped:

  • Expand education
  • Produce leaders
  • Support students
  • Establish institutions
  • Develop collective bargaining power
Limitations

They could also:

  • Reinforce caste identity
  • Encourage competition between communities
  • Replace universal equality with group advancement
  • Exclude women or poorer members

Community mobilisation was therefore both:

  • A method of social advancement
  • A continuation of caste-based organisation

The Nadar Mahajana Sangam remains an important example of organised educational and economic uplift.

Madras Labour Union and the Organised Labour Movement

The Madras Labour Union institutionalised collective bargaining among industrial workers and connected labour grievances with nationalism and the modern political public.

Industrial Background

Madras Presidency experienced the growth of:

  • Textile mills
  • Railways
  • Tramways
  • Ports
  • Printing presses
  • Petroleum installations
  • Engineering units
  • Municipal employment

Industrial workers faced:

  • Long working hours
  • Low wages
  • Unsafe conditions
  • Lack of job security
  • Racial discrimination
  • Harsh factory discipline
  • Absence of formal negotiation
Early Labour Protest

Workers had organised strikes before 1918, but most protests were temporary and lacked permanent institutions.

The Swadeshi period had already connected labour and nationalism through:

  • Coral Mills strike of 1908
  • V. O. Chidambaranar
  • Subramania Siva

Detailed Coral Mills history belongs to Chapter 17.

Madras Labour Union

The Madras Labour Union was established in:

  • April 1918

It represented workers of the:

  • Buckingham and Carnatic Mills
  • Commonly called Binny Mills

Important leaders included:

  • B. P. Wadia
  • Thiru. Vi. Kalyanasundaram
  • Other labour organisers

It is regarded as one of India’s earliest durable organised trade unions.

B. P. Wadia

B. P. Wadia was associated with:

  • Theosophical Society
  • Home Rule
  • Trade-union organisation
  • Workers’ education

He helped convert workplace grievances into structured union demands.

Thiru. Vi. Kalyanasundaram

Thiru. Vi. Ka. contributed through:

  • Labour speeches
  • Tamil journalism
  • Worker organisation
  • Nationalist politics
  • Negotiation with employers

He helped connect workers’ economic demands with the wider political public.

Buckingham and Carnatic Mills Disputes

The union organised workers around:

  • Wages
  • Hours of work
  • Working conditions
  • Dismissals
  • Right to organise

The major labour confrontations of the early 1920s showed both:

  • The strength of organised workers
  • The willingness of employers and government to suppress unions
Expansion of Trade Unions

Unions later emerged among:

  • Railway workers
  • Tramway workers
  • Printing workers
  • Municipal workers
  • Petroleum workers
  • Textile workers
  • Engineering workers
Importance

The organised labour movement introduced the idea that workers possessed:

  • Collective rights
  • Bargaining power
  • A shared class identity

Labour politics later developed into nationalist, socialist and communist streams.

Singaravelar, May Day and Socialist–Communist Currents

Singaravelar linked labour rights, May Day, peasant organisation, socialism, communism and anti-colonial politics in the Madras Presidency.

Singaravelar

M. Singaravelar lived from:

  • 1860 to 1946

He was associated with:

  • Labour organisation
  • Nationalism
  • Socialism
  • Communism
  • Rationalist thought
  • Municipal politics

He began his public career as a lawyer and became involved in the national movement.

Labour Activism

Singaravelar supported workers in industries including:

  • Textiles
  • Tramways
  • Electricity
  • Railways
  • Printing
  • Petroleum
  • Municipal services

He argued that political freedom should include:

  • Economic equality
  • Workers’ rights
  • Reduction of exploitation
  • Organisation of peasants and labourers
First May Day Celebration

On 1 May 1923, Singaravelar organised May Day meetings in Madras.

Important locations included:

  • Beach area near the Madras High Court
  • Triplicane beach

The events are widely regarded as the first organised May Day observance in India.

Important features included:

  • Use of the red flag
  • Demand for a May Day holiday
  • Call for worker unity
  • Speeches on labour rights
Labour Kisan Party of Hindustan

Singaravelar announced the:

  • Labour Kisan Party of Hindustan
  • On 1 May 1923

Its programme attempted to unite:

  • Industrial workers
  • Peasants
  • Anti-colonial activists
  • Socialist thinkers
Relationship with Nationalism

Singaravelar participated in:

  • Non-Cooperation
  • Boycott campaigns
  • Labour strikes
  • Anti-colonial protest

He later criticised the limitations of elite nationalism and emphasised class struggle.

Communist and Socialist Growth

Socialist and communist ideas spread through:

  • Labour unions
  • Study groups
  • Newspapers
  • Translations
  • Congress Socialist networks
  • Industrial centres

Important later leaders included:

  • P. Jeevanandham
  • P. Ramamurthi
  • B. Srinivasa Rao
  • M. R. Venkatraman
P. Jeevanandham

Jeevanandham moved through several ideological phases:

  • Gandhian nationalism
  • Anti-caste activity
  • Self-Respect Movement
  • Congress Socialist Party
  • Communist movement

He organised:

  • Industrial workers
  • Agricultural labourers
  • Rickshaw workers
  • Textile workers

His complete role in rationalism and Self-Respect politics should not be repeated here.

Importance

Singaravelar connected:

  • National independence
  • Labour rights
  • Socialism
  • Rational inquiry
  • International worker solidarity.
Peasant and Agricultural-Labour Movements

Peasant and agricultural-labour movements addressed rent, wages, landlessness, caste oppression and landlord power, especially in the Thanjavur delta.

Agrarian Structure

Rural Tamil society included:

  • Large landholders
  • Mirasdars
  • Tenants
  • Sharecroppers
  • Small cultivators
  • Bonded labourers
  • Landless agricultural workers

Caste and class were closely connected.

Many landless workers belonged to socially oppressed communities.

Major Grievances

Peasants and agricultural workers protested against:

  • High rents
  • Eviction
  • Low wages
  • Debt
  • Bonded labour
  • Forced or unpaid services
  • Caste humiliation
  • Denial of housing rights
  • Violence by landlords
Kisan Organisations

Peasant organisations expanded during the 1930s and 1940s.

They were influenced by:

  • Congress Socialist Party
  • Communist Party
  • All India Kisan Sabha
  • Local agricultural unions
Thanjavur Region

The Thanjavur delta became an important centre of agrarian mobilisation.

The region contained:

  • Productive wet-land agriculture
  • Powerful landlords
  • Large numbers of tenants and agricultural labourers
  • Severe caste-based inequalities

From the 1940s, organisers worked among:

  • Tenant cultivators
  • Farm servants
  • Landless workers
  • Dalit agricultural labourers
Important Leaders

Leaders associated with left and agrarian mobilisation included:

  • B. Srinivasa Rao
  • P. Jeevanandham
  • P. Ramamurthi
  • Local Kisan Sabha organisers
Methods

The movements used:

  • Wage strikes
  • Harvest-time mobilisation
  • Refusal of unpaid labour
  • Rent campaigns
  • Public meetings
  • Village unions
  • Legal petitions
  • Collective bargaining
Relationship between Caste and Class

Agricultural labourers often faced both:

  • Economic exploitation
  • Untouchability and social exclusion

The movements therefore addressed:

  • Wages
  • Land relations
  • Caste violence
  • Public dignity
Post-Independence Continuity

Agrarian struggles continued after 1947 and became important in the politics of the Cauvery delta.

This chapter provides only the twentieth-century origin. Detailed post-Independence agrarian conflicts require separate economic and political treatment.

Women’s Organisations, Suffrage and Public Participation

Women’s organisations transformed women from dependants into political citizens through suffrage, education, public participation and legislative advocacy.

Women’s India Association

The Women’s India Association was founded at:

  • Adyar, Madras
  • On 8 May 1917

Important founders included:

  • Annie Besant
  • Margaret Cousins
  • Dorothy Jinarajadasa

Other prominent participants included:

  • Muthulakshmi Reddy
  • Ammu Swaminathan
  • Ambujammal
  • Women from different religious and social backgrounds
Objectives

The association worked for:

  • Women’s education
  • Voting rights
  • Political representation
  • Legal equality
  • Marriage reform
  • Women’s health
  • Abolition of child marriage
  • Reform of the Devadasi system
  • Public participation
Stri Dharma

The Women’s India Association published:

  • Stri Dharma

The journal discussed:

  • Women’s rights
  • Political reform
  • Education
  • International women’s movements
  • Legislative questions
Women’s Franchise

The Government of India Act of 1919 allowed provincial legislatures to decide whether women could be enfranchised.

In 1921, the Madras Presidency became one of the earliest provinces to extend voting rights to women under prescribed qualifications.

Women later gained the right to stand for election.

All India Women’s Conference

The All India Women’s Conference was established in:

  • 1927

It began with a strong emphasis on:

  • Women’s education

It later addressed:

  • Child marriage
  • Legal reform
  • Property rights
  • Political participation
  • Health
  • Social welfare
Public Participation

Women entered public life as:

  • Voters
  • Legislators
  • Congress activists
  • Journalists
  • Teachers
  • Doctors
  • Social workers
  • Trade-union supporters
  • Speakers
Importance

Women’s organisations established that women were:

  • Political citizens
  • Independent rights-holders
  • Participants in legislation
  • Not merely dependants within households

Detailed women’s freedom-struggle activities belong to Chapter 19.

Muthulakshmi Reddy and Legislative Social Reform

Muthulakshmi Reddy used medicine, legislation and institution-building to pursue women’s education, public health and reform of Devadasi dedication.

Early Life

Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy was born in:

  • 1886
  • Pudukkottai

She became:

  • A doctor
  • Women’s-rights campaigner
  • Legislator
  • Social reformer
  • Institution builder
Legislative Position

She became:

  • The first woman nominated to the Madras Legislative Council
  • Deputy President of the Council

Her entry into the legislature demonstrated the connection between:

  • Women’s education
  • Suffrage
  • Organised women’s politics
  • Legal reform
Main Reform Areas

Muthulakshmi Reddy worked on:

  • Child marriage
  • Women’s education
  • Public health
  • Maternal care
  • Protection of girls
  • Devadasi dedication
  • Women’s legal status
  • Social welfare
Devadasi Reform

She campaigned against the dedication of girls to temples.

Her arguments emphasised:

  • Human dignity
  • Exploitation of women
  • Denial of ordinary family life
  • Health and welfare
  • The right to education and marriage

She introduced proposals for legal abolition during the late 1920s and early 1930s.

The final Madras Devadasis Prevention of Dedication Act was enacted in:

  • 1947

The law:

  • Prohibited dedication
  • Gave Devadasi women legal freedom to marry
  • Removed legal support for the institution
Avvai Home

Muthulakshmi Reddy founded:

  • Avvai Home
  • At Adyar

It provided support for:

  • Destitute girls
  • Women seeking education
  • Girls escaping exploitative conditions
Cancer Institute

Her later public-health legacy included the creation of the:

  • Cancer Institute at Adyar

This belongs mainly to her post-Independence contribution.

Civil Disobedience Protest

In 1930, she resigned from the Legislative Council in protest following Gandhi’s arrest during the Civil Disobedience Movement.

Historical Debate

The Devadasi reform movement included several different positions.

Some reformers regarded the system entirely as oppression.

Some women connected to hereditary performing communities feared that abolition without rehabilitation would destroy:

  • Livelihood
  • Artistic tradition
  • Property support

The reform must therefore be studied through both:

  • Women’s emancipation
  • Social consequences of legal abolition

Detailed women’s freedom-struggle participation belongs to Chapter 19.

Temple Entry and Anti-Untouchability Movements

Temple-entry and anti-untouchability campaigns challenged specific civil and religious exclusions, while radical critics argued that access alone could not abolish caste hierarchy.

Background

Untouchability restricted oppressed communities from:

  • Entering temples
  • Using public roads
  • Drawing water from common sources
  • Entering schools
  • Accessing public institutions
  • Participating equally in religious life

Temple entry became a symbol of:

  • Human equality
  • Civic rights
  • Religious access
  • Rejection of caste exclusion
Vaikom Satyagraha

The Vaikom Satyagraha occurred during:

  • 1924–1925
  • Travancore

The immediate issue was the prohibition imposed on oppressed communities from using roads surrounding the Vaikom temple.

Tamil leaders associated with the movement included:

  • E. V. Ramasamy
  • Nagammai
  • Kannammal
  • P. Jeevanandham and other volunteers

Periyar’s detailed contribution belongs to Chapter 28.

Suchindram and Other Campaigns

Anti-untouchability activity also developed around temples and public roads in the Tamil-speaking Travancore region.

Campaigners demanded:

  • Road access
  • Temple access
  • Equal civic treatment
Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation

In 1936, the ruler of Travancore issued the Temple Entry Proclamation.

It opened state-controlled Hindu temples to communities previously excluded by caste.

This proclamation applied to Travancore, including the present Kanyakumari region.

Madurai Meenakshi Temple Entry

On 8 July 1939, A. Vaidyanatha Iyer led a group into the Meenakshi Amman Temple at Madurai.

Participants included oppressed-caste volunteers and reform supporters.

P. Kakkan was among those associated with the entry.

Temple Entry Authorisation

The Madras government enacted the:

  • Temple Entry Authorisation and Indemnity Act
  • In 1939

The legislation protected temple authorities who permitted previously excluded communities to enter.

Different Approaches
Gandhian Reformers

They often used:

  • Satyagraha
  • Moral persuasion
  • Harijan service
  • Reform from within Hindu society
Self-Respect and Radical Anti-Caste Thinkers

They questioned whether temple entry alone could end:

  • Caste hierarchy
  • Priesthood inequality
  • Religious authority
  • Birth-based status
Importance

Temple entry was a major civil-rights achievement, but it did not automatically remove caste discrimination from:

  • Housing
  • Marriage
  • Employment
  • Education
  • Land ownership

Detailed rationalist criticism of religion belongs to Chapters 23, 24 and 28.

Pure Tamil Movement and Language-Based Identity

The Pure Tamil Movement converted linguistic scholarship into a wider programme of Tamil identity, educational advocacy and resistance to excessive Sanskrit influence.

Background

Tamil linguistic consciousness grew from nineteenth-century developments such as:

  • Classical-text recovery
  • Comparative Dravidian linguistics
  • Printing
  • Tamil scholarship
  • Growth of modern prose
  • Cultural revival

The twentieth century transformed literary interest into a broader socio-political language movement.

Pure Tamil Movement

The Pure Tamil Movement is known as:

  • Tanittamil Iyakkam

It promoted:

  • Use of Tamil words in place of Sanskrit-derived vocabulary
  • Tamil personal names
  • Tamil religious terminology
  • Tamil-medium expression
  • Recognition of Tamil antiquity
  • Linguistic self-respect
Maraimalai Adigal

Maraimalai Adigal was a major leader of the Pure Tamil Movement.

Important associations:

  • Saiva scholarship
  • Tanittamil
  • Tamil prose
  • Opposition to excessive Sanskrit influence
  • Tamil cultural identity

He adopted a Tamilised name in place of his earlier Sanskrit-influenced name.

Parithimar Kalaignar

V. G. Suryanarayana Sastri adopted the name:

  • Parithimar Kalaignar

He argued for:

  • Recognition of Tamil’s classical status
  • Greater importance for Tamil in higher education
  • Linguistic independence
Other Scholars

The movement was strengthened by writers and scholars such as:

  • Devaneya Pavanar
  • Thiru. Vi. Ka.
  • Bharathidasan
  • Tamil teachers and journal editors
Social and Political Effects

The Pure Tamil Movement influenced:

  • Public names
  • Journalism
  • Political speeches
  • Organisational terminology
  • Tamil-medium education
  • Criticism of Sanskrit dominance
  • Dravidian cultural identity
Limitations

Pure Tamil was easier to use in:

  • Formal writing
  • Speeches
  • Literary production

than in all forms of everyday language.

Critics argued that extreme linguistic purification could:

  • Reduce accessibility
  • Ignore the historical mixing of languages
  • Replace one linguistic hierarchy with another
Chapter Boundary

Detailed literary contributions belong to Chapter 7.

This topic focuses only on the movement’s role in:

  • Identity
  • Education
  • Public politics
  • Social mobilisation
Anti-Hindi Agitations and Language Politics

Anti-Hindi agitations turned language policy into mass politics by linking Tamil, education, employment and federal autonomy.

Background

Language became a political issue because it affected:

  • Education
  • Government employment
  • Cultural identity
  • Provincial autonomy
  • Relations with the Indian Union

Tamil activists feared that compulsory Hindi could reduce the status of:

  • Tamil
  • Tamil-medium education
  • Non-Hindi speakers
Compulsory Hindi Policy

After the Congress ministry came to power in the Madras Presidency in 1937, Premier C. Rajagopalachari introduced compulsory Hindi instruction in selected secondary schools.

Supporters argued that Hindi would:

  • Promote Indian unity
  • Improve communication across regions

Opponents argued that it represented:

  • Cultural domination
  • Additional educational burden
  • Discrimination against non-Hindi speakers
  • A threat to Tamil
First Anti-Hindi Agitation

The agitation began in:

  • 1937

Important leaders included:

  • E. V. Ramasamy
  • Somasundara Bharathiar
  • Maraimalai Adigal
  • K. A. P. Viswanatham
  • Justice Party leaders
  • Tamil scholars
  • Women activists
Methods

The movement used:

  • Public meetings
  • Conferences
  • School picketing
  • Processions
  • Pamphlets
  • Hunger strikes
  • Arrest campaigns
  • Women’s participation
Natarajan and Thalamuthu

Two young activists remembered as language martyrs were:

  • Natarajan
  • Thalamuthu

They died after imprisonment during the agitation.

Their names are often stated together as:

  • Thalamuthu–Natarajan

Chronologically, Natarajan died before Thalamuthu.

Withdrawal

The compulsory-Hindi order was withdrawn in:

  • 1940

after the Congress ministry had resigned and the province came under Governor’s rule.

Anti-Hindi Agitation of 1965

A second major language agitation occurred in:

  • 1965

It opposed the feared replacement of English by Hindi as the sole official language of the Union.

Major features included:

  • Student participation
  • Statewide protests
  • Self-immolation by some protesters
  • Police action
  • Stronger support for Dravidian parties
  • Assurance of continued English use
Historical Distinction
1937–1940 Agitation
  • Against compulsory Hindi in provincial schools
  • Directed mainly against the Rajaji ministry’s education policy
1965 Agitation
  • Against possible exclusive use of Hindi at the Union level
  • Closely connected with official-language policy
  • Major factor in the rise of DMK

Detailed Dravidian organisation and Anna’s role belong to Chapters 25, 27 and 29.

Transition to Rationalist, Self-Respect and Dravidian Politics

From the 1920s to the 1940s, representation politics broadened into rationalism, Self-Respect, Dravidar Kazhagam and eventually electoral Dravidian politics.

Limits of Early Non-Brahmin Politics

The early non-Brahmin movement concentrated mainly on:

  • Government employment
  • Education
  • Representation
  • Administrative opportunity

By the 1920s, younger and more radical activists argued that representation alone could not eliminate:

  • Caste hierarchy
  • Gender inequality
  • Religious authority
  • Social humiliation
  • Economic exploitation
Growth of Rationalist Thought

Rationalist thinkers questioned:

  • Superstition
  • Scriptural authority
  • Birth-based status
  • Priesthood monopoly
  • Religious justification of caste
  • Unequal treatment of women

Important early contributors included:

  • Iyothee Thass
  • Singaravelar
  • Periyar
  • P. Jeevanandham
  • Rationalist writers and journals

Detailed growth of rationalism belongs to Chapter 23.

Self-Respect Movement

The Self-Respect Movement emerged in:

  • 1925

It was led principally by:

  • E. V. Ramasamy

It promoted:

  • Self-respect
  • Caste equality
  • Women’s rights
  • Rationalism
  • Inter-caste marriage
  • Marriage without Brahmin priests
  • Criticism of religious hierarchy

Detailed history belongs to Chapter 24.

Its principles belong to Chapter 26.

Periyar’s complete role belongs to Chapter 28.

Justice Party and Periyar

Periyar gradually became associated with the Justice Party during the 1930s.

The party’s political organisation and the Self-Respect Movement’s social ideology increasingly influenced one another.

In 1944, the Justice Party was transformed into:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam

The organisation:

  • Withdrew from electoral politics
  • Emphasised social revolution
  • Promoted rationalism
  • Opposed caste hierarchy
  • Advocated Dravidian identity
Formation of DMK

In 1949, a group led by:

  • C. N. Annadurai

separated from Dravidar Kazhagam and founded:

  • Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam
  • DMK

The differences involved:

  • Electoral participation
  • Organisational strategy
  • Political methods
  • Leadership questions
Expansion through Public Culture

Dravidian politics used:

  • Newspapers
  • Public meetings
  • Theatre
  • Cinema
  • Novels
  • Short stories
  • Songs
  • Political dialogues
Post-Independence Transformation

The Dravidian movement influenced:

  • Reservation
  • Language policy
  • State autonomy
  • Social welfare
  • Tamil cultural identity
  • Electoral politics
  • Public communication

The DMK formed the government in Madras State in:

  • 1967

This topic provides only the transition.

Detailed treatment is reserved for:

  • Chapter 25 — Dravidian Movement

  • Chapter 27 — Principles of Dravidian Movement

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, leaders, organisations, publications and distinctions across non-Brahmin, Adi Dravida, labour, women’s, language and Dravidian movements.

High-Yield Distinctions
Non-Brahmin Movement versus Adi Dravida Movement

Non-Brahmin movement

  • Broader coalition of communities outside Brahmin groups
  • Public employment
  • Education
  • Political representation
  • Justice Party

Adi Dravida movement

  • Focused on communities subjected to untouchability
  • Civil rights
  • Education
  • Separate political safeguards
  • Anti-caste identity

The two movements sometimes cooperated but were not identical.

Madras Non-Brahmin Association versus Madras United League

Madras Non-Brahmin Association

  • 1909
  • Early political association
  • Limited organisational reach

Madras United League

  • 1912
  • Included government employees
  • Developed into the Madras Dravidian Association
Madras Dravidian Association versus Justice Party

Madras Dravidian Association

  • Educational and social organisation
  • Dravidian Home
  • Precursor organisation

Justice Party

  • Political party
  • Contested elections
  • Formed provincial ministries
Justice Party versus South Indian Liberal Federation

They refer to the same principal organisation:

  • Official name — South Indian Liberal Federation
  • Popular name — Justice Party
Communal Representation versus Universal Equality

Communal representation

  • Group-based allocation
  • Corrective response to historical exclusion

Universal equality

  • Same formal rule for everyone
  • May ignore unequal starting conditions
M. C. Rajah versus Rettamalai Srinivasan

M. C. Rajah

  • Legislative representation
  • Rajah–Moonje Pact
  • Adi Dravida political safeguards

Rettamalai Srinivasan

  • Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha
  • Paraiyan newspaper
  • Round Table Conference participation
Madras Labour Union versus Labour Kisan Party

Madras Labour Union

  • Trade union
  • 1918
  • Buckingham and Carnatic Mills workers

Labour Kisan Party

  • Political labour–peasant organisation
  • 1923
  • Singaravelar
B. P. Wadia versus Singaravelar

B. P. Wadia

  • Madras Labour Union
  • Theosophy and Home Rule background
  • Early trade-union organisation

Singaravelar

  • May Day
  • Labour Kisan Party
  • Socialist and communist politics
Industrial Labour versus Agricultural Labour

Industrial labour

  • Mills
  • Railways
  • Tramways
  • Ports
  • Factories

Agricultural labour

  • Rural
  • Landless work
  • Tenant and wage struggles
  • Closely linked with caste hierarchy
Women’s India Association versus All India Women’s Conference

Women’s India Association

  • 1917
  • Adyar
  • Suffrage and broad women’s rights

All India Women’s Conference

  • 1927
  • Began with education
  • Expanded into legal and social reform
Muthulakshmi Reddy versus Rukmini Lakshmipathi

Muthulakshmi Reddy

  • Doctor
  • Legislator
  • Devadasi reform
  • Women’s welfare

Rukmini Lakshmipathi

  • Congress activist
  • Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha
  • Imprisonment
  • Later minister
Temple Entry versus Caste Abolition

Temple entry

  • Access to worship
  • Removal of a specific civil disability

Caste abolition

  • Removal of the entire birth-based hierarchy
  • Includes marriage, occupation, education and social status

Temple entry alone did not abolish caste.

Pure Tamil Movement versus Anti-Hindi Movement

Pure Tamil Movement

  • Internal reform of Tamil vocabulary
  • Reduction of Sanskrit influence
  • Cultural and literary identity

Anti-Hindi Movement

  • Opposition to compulsory or dominant Hindi
  • Education and official-language politics
First versus Second Anti-Hindi Agitation

1937–1940

  • Compulsory Hindi in Madras Presidency schools
  • Rajaji ministry

1965

  • Union official-language issue
  • Student mobilisation
  • Strengthened DMK
Justice Party versus Self-Respect Movement

Justice Party

  • Electoral political organisation
  • Representation and government policy

Self-Respect Movement

  • Social movement
  • Caste, religion, marriage and gender reform
Dravidar Kazhagam versus DMK

Dravidar Kazhagam

  • 1944
  • Periyar
  • Non-electoral social movement

DMK

  • 1949
  • Anna
  • Electoral political party
Exam Traps
  • Madras Non-Brahmin Association was founded before the Justice Party.
  • Madras United League developed into the Madras Dravidian Association.
  • C. Natesa Mudaliar is associated with the Dravidian Home.
  • South Indian Liberal Federation is the official name of the Justice Party.
  • The Non-Brahmin Manifesto belongs to 1916.
  • Justice newspaper began in 1917.
  • Nadar Mahajana Sangam was established in 1910.
  • Madras Labour Union was formed in 1918.
  • Singaravelar organised May Day in Madras on 1 May 1923.
  • Labour Kisan Party was not the same as Madras Labour Union.
  • Women’s India Association was founded at Adyar in 1917.
  • Madras extended qualified women’s franchise in 1921.
  • Muthulakshmi Reddy is associated with Devadasi abolition and women’s welfare.
  • Vaikom Satyagraha concerned access to roads surrounding a temple.
  • Madurai Meenakshi Temple Entry occurred on 8 July 1939.
  • The first Anti-Hindi agitation began in 1937.
  • Natarajan and Thalamuthu are associated with the first Anti-Hindi agitation.
  • Justice Party became Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.
  • DMK was founded in 1949.
